parts:
Hi, I'm trying to use a mixture model to estimate the proportion and mixture of two sources of error in tree dbh growth.
The first error which affects the majority of the data is small errors associated with measuring dbh and varies with the size of the plant. The second error is a larger size independent error that could arise from measuring the wrong tree.

The data I plan to fit this mixture model to is a dataset where trees are measured twice in a period where we do not expect any growth.

Now this is the first time I've attempted to run such a model. So I thought I'd first simulate it. The problem I've found is that the model seems to be extremely sensitive to the choice of prior... which isn't very helpful when I actually attempt to fit the real data.


#GENERATE DATA

dbh <- rlnorm(n_obs, 3.443309, 0.9253412)
sda <- 0.927
sdb <- 0.0038
SD2 <- 25.6
theta <- 0.028
true_val <- 0

sim <- c(rnorm(n_obs*(1-theta), true_val, sda + sdb*dbh), rnorm(n_obs*theta, true_val, SD2))

model <- '
data {
int<lower=1> n_obs;
vector[n_obs] sim;
vector[n_obs] dbh;
}

real<lower=0, upper=0.1> sdb;
real<lower=0, upper=40> SD2;
real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;

  log_theta <- log(theta);
  log1m_theta <- log1m(theta);

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: Mixture model & priors
parts:
I think this is a case of label switching. In the second model, theta (approximately) equals 1-theta from the first model. Also, the order of magnitude of the standard errors of the two mixture components have switched. The cause is the use of rather wide priors in the second model (relative to the first model), which allow for multimodality in the posterior (and thus, label switching).

It may or may not be coincidence that in the second model, all three chains explored the area around the same mode.

Anyway, in the second model I would adopt more informative priors for sda, sdb, and SD2 that reflect your knowledge about the second source of error being larger than the first (a Cauchy prior is rather vague). E.g.:
sda ~ normal(0, 3)
sdb ~  normal(0, 0.1)
SD2 ~ normal(0, 10)

By the way, you can drop the truncation terms in the second model ("T[,]"), as the parameters of the prior are fixed (and thus also is the adjustment of the posterior, which we can therefore ignore).

messages.subject: Re: Mixture model & priors
parts:
Haha, worse still, I meant sdb < sda < SD2. But you got the idea :).

I don't think you need to change anything about the parameter theta. I tried adding informative priors for elements of the ordered vector sigma:

sigma[1] ~ normal(0, 0.01);
sigma[2] ~ normal(0,1);
sigma[3] ~ normal(0,25);

And by chance, the NUTS sampler sometimes now ends up in the mode that corresponds with you data-generating process. So it seems that some unidentifiability remains. Adding prior information for theta may work

theta ~ beta(10,90);  // on its own still doesn't work.

Restricting the support for theta to <lower=0,upper=0.25> made an end to the multimodality. I first tried an upper bound of 0.5, but then the sampler sometimes started hugging and clinging to it. This model seems to be not very well behaved :).

So the final model that worked for me was:

model <- '
data {
int<lower=1> n_obs;
vector[n_obs] sim;
vector[n_obs] dbh;
}
parameters {
real<lower=0, upper=.25> theta;

positive_ordered[3] sigma; # sort sigmas from smallest to largest - helps with switching issues
}
model {

sigma[1] ~ normal(0, 0.01);
sigma[2] ~ normal(0,1);
sigma[3] ~ normal(0,25);

for (i in 1:n_obs) {
   increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log1m(theta) + normal_log(sim[i], 0, sigma[2] + sigma[1] * dbh[i]), #most of data
                                  log(theta) + normal_log(sim[i], 0, sigma[3])));  #few data
 }
}'

I then extracted the estimated sigma's and theta associated with this model and incorporated them as fixed parameters in another model fitted to a much larger dataset (180,000 observations) where we did not know true dbh. This model works fine when applied to small amounts of data (>500 observations), with parameters quickly converging, and after 2000 iterations reasonable effective samples (>100).
The problem I've seemed to run into is when I apply this model to the whole dataset. Sampling/warmup seems to be taking forever... (approximately 4 minutes per iteration)

I knew using a larger dataset would slow things down... but not by this much.
The priors I have set on the mu's are all quiet tight. I guess the half cauchy priors on the sigma's might be too wide... but I've also tried just tried constraining these to be between 0 and 10 and it hasn't seemed to help.

I’m not exactly sure what you are expecting — 4 minutes per iteration for
a big model like this is pretty fast.  Especially when you consider that
with that much data your posterior is likely concentrating on some very
small neighborhood, and if you have any non-identifiabilities that
neighborhood will be a thin, warped surface that requires a very small
step size to explore adequately.  The I/O overhead can be substantial,
especially if you’re using RStan or PyStan, and you might want to 
run from CmdStan to focus computational resources on sampling alone.

You want to do as much algebra as you can on the inside
to avoid log exp log round trips. So instead of

true_dbh1[i] <- exp(log_raw_true_dbh1[i] * log_sigma_true_dbh1 + log_mu_true_dbh1);
dbh_increment <- exp(log_raw_dbh_increment[i] * log_sigma_dbh_increment + log_mu_dbh_increment);
true_dbh2[i] <- true_dbh1[i] + dbh_increment;
dbh_dt_rel[i] <- (log(true_dbh2[i]) - log(true_dbh1[i]))/census_length[i];

I'd recommend the following for arithmetic stability:

log_true_dbh1[i] <- log_raw_true_dbh1[i] * log_sigma_true_dbh1 + log_mu_true_dbh1
log_dbh_inc <- log_raw_dbh_inc[i] * log_sigma_dbh_inc + log_mu_dbh_inc;
log_true_dbh2[i] <- log_sum_exp(log_true_dbh1[i], log_dbh_inc)
dbh_dt_rel[i] <- (log_true_dbh2[i] - log_true_dbh1[i]) / census_length[i];

It may not make a difference if the values of true_dbh1 are well behaved and small.

Also, for binary mixtures, we have a log_mix function:

log_mix(theta, lp1, lp2)

=def= log_sum_exp(log(theta) + lp1,
log1m(theta) + lp2);

which should be a bit cleaner and also should be a bit more efficient.

You don't ever want to compute anything twice, so this
> basal_area_dt[i] <- (0.25*pi()*true_dbh2[i]^2 - 0.25*pi()*true_dbh1[i]^2)/census_length[i];

implies you want to define

transformed data {
real quarter_pi;
quarter_pi = 0.25 * pi();

And never multiply twice when you can use distributivity, and use
square(a) instead of a^2, so that'd be:

basal_area_dt[i] <- quarter_pi * (square(true_dbh2[i]) - square(true_dbh1[i]))
/ census_length[i];

Now you can see that you can get away with even more up front
optimization by defining

transformed_data {
vector[n_obs] quarter_pi_over_census_length;
quarter_pi_over_census_length <- quarter_pi / census_length[i];

and then

basal_area_dt[i] <- quarter_pi_over_census_length[i] * (square(true_dbh2[i]) - square(true_dbh1[i]))

Any time you can cut down repetivie multiplications, it's a big
win. Not so big in generated quantities, but still worthwhile.

Saving all those generated quantities is also expensive. They could
be printed outside the model, but that's a huge pain.

I don't know what you expect the values of those standard deviations
with (0,10) uniform priors, but we generally recommend just (0, inf)
constraints with at least a weakly informative prior around where you
expect the value to be. This can help a lot computationally if the
value's expected to be around 1. You can even use something like
normal(1,1) if you expect it to be in (0, 2) but want to allow it to
be bigger if there's enough data.

- Bob

parts:
Thanks Bob,
I've implemented most of the changes you recommended.
One change I haven't implement was leaving true_dbh1 on the log scale. This is because the parameters in the mixture models need to be on the normal scale, and if I implemented your suggestion I'd need to exp(log_true_dbh1) within the mixture model. Also I'm not getting any informational warnings with running this model so I don't think I'm running into overflow/underflow problems.

One thing I have noticed is that the model runs MUCH faster without the non-centered reparameterisations of the lognormals (200 seconds vs 1400 seconds) when running 2000 iterations with only 1000 observations.
I've also noticed that the non-centered version of the model seems to struggle to converge with more data added - I tested the models below on 100 obs, 500 obs and 1000 obs... and progressively watched the effective samples decrease and rhat's increase in the non-centered version. This isn't seen in the model without this reparameterisation - if anything effective samples increase with more data. 
I found this surprising as I thought the non-centered approach would either have little effect on the sampling or improve it... I didn't consider it could make things worse. Maybe this is just an issue with the lognormal reparameterisation?

I guess a more general question that users would be interested in is when should one use the non-centered parameterisation? I was under the impression that if you're building complex hierarchical models it's pretty much a safe bet that you'll see an improvement (i.e. as outlined in the FAQ).  But does it increase computational time? and are the benefits diminished with large datasets? 


Model without non-centered reparameterisations:

data {
      int<lower=1> n_obs;
      vector[n_obs] census_length;
      vector[n_obs] obs_dbh1;
      vector[n_obs] obs_dbh2;
    }

transformed data {
  real quarter_pi;
  quarter_pi <- 0.25 *pi();
  }
  
  parameters {
    real<lower=0> true_dbh1[n_obs];
    real log_mu_true_dbh1;
    real<lower=0> log_sigma_true_dbh1;

    real<lower=0> log_sigma_dbh_increment;
  }
  
  model {
  
    real true_dbh2[n_obs];
    
    true_dbh1 ~ lognormal(log_mu_true_dbh1, log_sigma_true_dbh1);
    dbh_increment ~ lognormal(log_mu_dbh_increment, log_sigma_dbh_increment);

for (i in 1:n_obs) {
      // Calculating true growth for fitted data
true_dbh2[i] <- true_dbh1[i] + dbh_increment[i];
// theta and SDs are fixed and where determined from another model on data explicitly collected to examine measurement error

increment_log_prob(log_mix(0.046908,normal_log(obs_dbh1[i], true_dbh1[i], 3.496852),
                                  normal_log(obs_dbh1[i], true_dbh1[i], 0.085871 + 0.005716 * true_dbh1[i]))); 
      
      increment_log_prob(log_mix(0.046908, normal_log(obs_dbh2[i], true_dbh2[i], 3.496852), 
                                 normal_log(obs_dbh2[i], true_dbh2[i], 0.085871 + 0.005716 * true_dbh2[i])));  
    }
    // Priors
    
    log_mu_true_dbh1 ~ normal(0,5);
    log_sigma_true_dbh1 ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

    log_mu_dbh_increment ~ normal(0,5);
    log_sigma_dbh_increment ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
    
  }



*Model with non-centered reparameterisation*

data {
  int<lower=1> n_obs;
  vector[n_obs] census_length;
  vector[n_obs] obs_dbh1;
  vector[n_obs] obs_dbh2;
  }

transformed data {

  }
  
  model {

real true_dbh1[n_obs];
  real true_dbh2[n_obs];
real dbh_increment[n_obs];
for (i in 1:n_obs) {
// Calculating true growth for fitted data

true_dbh1[i] <- exp(log_mu_true_dbh1 + log_sigma_true_dbh1 * raw_true_dbh1[i]);
  dbh_increment[i] <- exp(log_mu_dbh_increment + log_sigma_dbh_increment * raw_dbh_increment[i]);
  true_dbh2[i] <- true_dbh1[i] + dbh_increment[i];
// theta and SDs are fixed and where determined from another model on data explicitly collected to examine measurement error

increment_log_prob(log_mix(0.046908,normal_log(obs_dbh1[i], true_dbh1[i], 3.496852),
  normal_log(obs_dbh1[i], true_dbh1[i], 0.085871 + 0.005716 * true_dbh1[i]))); 
  
  increment_log_prob(log_mix(0.046908, normal_log(obs_dbh2[i], true_dbh2[i], 3.496852), 
  normal_log(obs_dbh2[i], true_dbh2[i], 0.085871 + 0.005716 * true_dbh2[i])));  
  }
  // Priors
  raw_true_dbh1 ~ normal(0,1);

parts:
Hi again. I'm finding that a few (e.g. <5%) of the true_dbh1 posteriors aren't fully converging (all hyper parameters converge nicely).
It appears that in some cases there might be two modes...
I know this can be a problem with mixture models and determining convergence can be difficult. But I was wondering what the best solution would be. The manual recommends running a single chain or setting initials around a single mode - but as you can see one chain can switch between modes easily.
I've tried lowering the stepsize and increasing adapt_delta but that doesn't really help. 

All I really need from this model is a point estimate of what true dbh1 and true dbh2 are so that it they can be used in another more complex model.
Would it be reasonable to use the medians despite this multimodal issue? or is there some other reparameterisation that might help?

for (i in 1:n_obs) {

increment_log_prob(log_mix(0.047,normal_log(obs_dbh1[i], true_dbh1[i], 3.498),

      increment_log_prob(log_mix(0.047, normal_log(obs_dbh2[i], true_dbh2[i], 3.498),

for (i in 1:n_obs) {
